newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Safras sees 2.51 mln tonne Brazil 97/98 wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: Safras sees 2.51 mln tonne Brazil 97/98 wheat crop.

text.p: Brazil's 1997/98 wheat harvest is set to drop 20 percent to 2.51 million tonnes from 3.13 million tonnes in 1996/97, independent consultants Safras e Mercado said.

Planted area will drop 17 percent to 1.51 million hectares from 1.82 million hectares in 1996, mainly due to low prices and the difficulty of selling this season's crop, Safras said. Productivity is set to be around 1,661 kilos per hectare.
"The main reason for producers' pessimism is the commercialization of the current harvest," Safras said in a weekly report.

The 1996/97 harvest was marked by a drop in prices and the government had to intervene to guarantee growers a minimum price, but official measures to stimulate the sector in 1997 provided some cause for optimism.

In particular, farmers were encouraged by the government maintaining a minimum price of 157 reais ($148) per tonne and signalling it would intervene to help the sale of the domestic harvest, as it did this season through subsidized auctions.

"Even so, the most important factor to avoid a drastic reduction in planted area would be through new import rules, which restrict financing, putting national production on an equal footing with external product," Safras said.
Of the producing states, Parana will account for 62 percent of the total Brazilian crop with a planted area of 890,000 hectares, compared with 1.1 million hectares in 1996.
Problems with the winter corn harvest due to drought is causing farmers to revert to planting wheat in some regions, Safras said.

The high profitability of the soybean crop meant growers were also more financially secure and thus more likely to plant a winter crop, which has the added advantage of keeping soil fertility intact for the next summer harvest.
Rio Grande do Sul will account for 32 percent of Brazil's total wheat crop, with a planted area of 511,000 hectares, down 10 percent from last year.

Producers there were expected to opt for wheat because of a lack of alternatives for the winter crop, but a drop in the soybean crop due to drought means the government will have to intervene in order to generate more interest in growing wheat.

Supply and demand should be tighter in 1997/98. "The reduction in domestic production and the restrictions to the financing of imports should modify the rhythm of miller purchasing, with a reflection in ending stocks," Safras said.

The rules, announced by Brazil last month, should reduce wheat imports by two percent to 5.65 million tonnes this season but the impact should be limited because of concessions to Brazil's partners in the Mercosur customs union.
"However, for the 1997/98 commercial year the situation should change, with the commercialization attempting to adapt itself to the new rules," Safras said.
Millers are likely to increase the frequency of purchases to avoid liquidity problems and imports should increase by only one percent despite the drop in the domestic crop.

National industrial demand was forecast to drop to 8.2 million tonnes from 8.3 million tonnes this season and ending stocks should be 469,200 tonnes compared to 693,100 tonnes in the current crop year, Safras said.

The 1996/97 Argentine crop should rise to 15.8 million tonnes compared to 9.45 million tonnes in the previous year. Due to rains, mostly in the south, only 14.5 million tonnes will be suitable for milling with the rest destined for feeding.

Argentina is expected to export 10.4 million tonnes, including 400,000 tonnes of feed wheat. Internal demand is seen at 4.7 million tonnes leaving ending stocks of 398,000 tonnes, enough for about one month's consumption.
